title: The smallest l/v that still ends in a long-mode takeoff
question: Short-mode takeoff is the fast escape and needs no wing raise; long mode needs four consecutive raising ticks first. A fast approach (small l/v) crosses the GF threshold early, so it should always take the short mode. What is the smallest l/v that still ends in a long-mode takeoff?
how_found: Exhaustive search of the grid l/v in {1.0, 1.1, ..., 20.0} ms x azimuth in {-90, -89, ..., 90} degrees: 34,571 episodes, 12,051 of which end in a long-mode takeoff. Of those, the smallest l/v, then the smallest azimuth.

geometry.note: Angular size and expansion speed at the first and last tick, in degrees and degrees per second. Each host computes these with its own atan and tan, so they are compared with a tolerance and are not part of trace.sha256.

notes: The boundary is not monotonic in l/v: on this grid only 8.8, 9.3 and 9.4 ms produce a long mode below 9.5 ms. At the same azimuth, 8.9 through 9.2 ms end in a short-mode takeoff.

Azimuth 31 degrees is the first degree outside the modelled 30-degree binocular overlap, so only the right eye sees the stimulus. In MaleCNS v1.0 the right giant fiber receives fewer LC4 and LPLC2 synapses than the left (55 and 91 cells against 71 and 94), so the right eye alone is the weakest drive the model has: weak enough to raise wings for four ticks before the GF pathway crosses.
The mirror stimulus at azimuth -31 degrees, seen by the stronger left eye alone, ends in a short-mode takeoff instead.
